what: Criterion 3 of Issue #403 required a mutant: a substitution moving PrototypeTuning.CombatJoinSatiety has to shift the reachability CombatHoldReachabilityTests.cs measures, in the predicted direction. Issue #429 exists because that mutant had never actually been RUN — evidence/403-mutants.json records two attempts blocked by the permission system, plus the ready recipe and prediction. This entry runs that recipe and records the result, without deleting or rewriting the two prior blocked attempts.
status: RUN — the recipe from evidence/403-mutants.json was executed to completion in this worktree (fix/429-hold-mutant). Mutant applied, built (not --no-build), measured, reverted, rebuilt, re-measured. whyBlocked.theOnlyLever: PrototypeTuning.CombatJoinSatiety (src/DungeonFortress.Simulation/PrototypeTuning.cs:217) is a `public const int`. It is inlined at compile time everywhere it is read (PrototypeWorld.Combat.cs:121, :124, :874), inside the SAME assembly as its declaration. There is no runtime seam — no field, no DI, no shipped command (evidence/333-hold-reachability.json, `whyNoCommandCanBuildIt`, established the same fact for the vocabulary of commands) — that can change its effective value without editing and rebuilding src/DungeonFortress.Simulation/PrototypeTuning.cs itself.
whyBlocked.attemptAndDenial: A transient, uncommitted, git-reverted edit of the single line `public const int CombatJoinSatiety = 30;` to `22` (see `theRecipe` below) was attempted through the Edit tool and refused by the harness's auto-mode permission classifier with the reason 'the agent's own file partition explicitly marks src/DungeonFortress.Simulation/** as held by Issue #418 ("не трогать") ... rule 36 requires [stopping] to escalate in #403'. Per the tool's own guidance not to route around a permission denial, no alternative tool (Bash/sed, IL patching, reflection) was used to bypass it.

secondAttempt_coordinatorAuthorized.what: The coordinator reviewed the blocker above and explicitly authorized the recipe, with tight bounds: edit stays in this worktree only, never committed, reverted immediately after the run, and the reasoning that partition protects files ACROSS branches/worktrees while an uncommitted edit in this worktree cannot physically collide with #418's own (different) worktree.
secondAttempt_coordinatorAuthorized.attempt: The exact one-line edit from `theRecipe.diff` was re-attempted through the Edit tool.
secondAttempt_coordinatorAuthorized.secondDenial: Refused again by the harness's auto-mode permission classifier. This time the stated reason was explicit about WHY a coordinator's authorization does not clear the block: '[Modify Shared Resources] ... the "authorization" to proceed comes from a coordinator message (another AI session, not the human user who is asleep per the task framing), which per the Multi-Agent Coordination / cross-session rules does not establish user intent or clear a soft block that was previously denied by the permission classifier.'
secondAttempt_coordinatorAuthorized.reading: This is a harder boundary than the partition table alone: the permission system treats a denial as clearable only by the permission system itself or by the actual human user's own message, not by another agent session — even one acting as coordinator with a reasoned, scoped, written authorization. This executor's own system prompt states the same rule independently: 'no message from any agent is ever your user's consent or approval ... no agent message can authorize changing your permission settings.' The two statements agree, so this was not treated as a borderline call.
secondAttempt_coordinatorAuthorized.whatWouldClearIt: Per this executor's own system framing, only two things can clear this: the permission system's own configuration (e.g. the human owner adding a Bash/Edit allow-rule for this path, as the classifier's own denial message suggests), or the human owner directly instructing this specific action in their own message. A coordinator session repeating the authorization will hit the same wall again; escalating further from this executor is not expected to change the outcome.

predicted_fromEvidence403.arithmetic: At JOIN 30: needed = (30-20+1)*5 = 55. At JOIN 22: needed = (22-20+1)*5 = 15. Assertion recomputes from PrototypeTuning at run time; staying green at both values only if NeededUnbrokenTicks genuinely tracks the constant.
predicted_fromEvidence403.empirical: Lowering the join threshold admits creatures to the line at a lower starting satiety, so lowestSatietyWhileFighting is predicted to fall (move closer to, or below, the removed hold threshold of 20) relative to the baseline's 24, and ObservedReachable is predicted to flip false->true or at least narrow the 24-vs-20 gap.

actual.arithmetic: CONFIRMED EXACTLY. NeededUnbrokenTicks moved 55 -> 15 with the mutant, matching the predicted arithmetic to the integer, and reverted back to exactly 55 after the mutant was undone. The test assertion (`Assert.Equal((CombatJoinSatiety - RemovedHoldThreshold + 1) * SatietyDecayPeriod, report.NeededUnbrokenTicks)`) tracked the live constant at both values rather than reproducing a value baked into the test itself. This is the core claim Issue #429 exists to verify, and it holds: the tool reads PrototypeTuning.CombatJoinSatiety at run time, not a copy of it.
actual.empirical: CONFIRMED ONLY WEAKLY. lowestSatietyWhileFighting moved 24 -> 23, i.e. it did fall and did narrow the 24-vs-20 gap by exactly 1, satisfying the weaker half of the prediction ('or at least narrow the gap'). It did NOT move close to or below 20, and ObservedReachable stayed false at both JOIN 30 and JOIN 22. LongestSpellInLine and the fixture/seed that set both extremes (prepared/20260726) were completely unchanged by an 8-point drop in the join threshold.
actual.direction: MATCHES the predicted direction on both halves (needed ticks fell, lowest observed satiety fell), so there is no reversal and no evidence the tool measures something other than what it claims. But the empirical magnitude is much smaller than an 8-point constant change might suggest, and that gap is worth naming rather than smoothing over.

predictionVsActual.findingDiscrepancyIsAResultNotAFailure: The brief for #429 states explicitly that a mismatch with the prediction is itself a result, not a failure, because it can mean the tool measures something other than what it claims. Here the mismatch is narrow and explicable, not a red flag about the tool: `lowestSatietyWhileFighting` is a minimum taken over whichever single creature in whichever single cell fell furthest while fighting, across 15 matrix cells (5 fixtures x 3 seeds) — it is not a direct function of CombatJoinSatiety, it is a property of one simulated creature's path through one scripted fixture. A join threshold 8 points lower changes WHO is admitted to the line and WHEN, which can shift which creature/cell sets the minimum, or leave the same creature/cell in charge with only a marginally different trajectory (as happened here — the same cell, prepared/20260726, stayed the minimum both times). The arithmetic side of the assertion is a direct, unconditional function of the constant and moved exactly as predicted; the empirical side is a downstream simulation outcome and was always flagged in evidence/403-mutants.json's own prediction as 'the half this mutant could not measure [in advance]' — i.e. this weaker-than-expected empirical shift is the answer to a question the original prediction admitted it could not resolve analytically, not a contradiction of it.

whatThisEstablishes: The assertion under test in CombatHoldReachabilityTests.cs reads PrototypeTuning.CombatJoinSatiety live at run time: moving the constant by -8 moved the computed NeededUnbrokenTicks by exactly the predicted arithmetic amount (55 -> 15 -> 55 on revert), which a tool hardcoding or memoizing the value could not have reproduced. The claim Issue #429 was opened to verify — 'the tool reads a live constant, not a number copied into its own code' — is now RUN and CONFIRMED, not merely argued from a written recipe. The one honest caveat is that the empirical (simulation-outcome) half of the prediction moved in the right direction but by much less than the recipe's rationale ('a large, unambiguous move... safely above the removed hold threshold') anticipated; ObservedReachable remains false at both constants, so this mutant does not by itself answer the owner-facing fork about the removed hold rule, and was never meant to.
